description.narrative: Bangladesh Health Watch (BHW) is a civil society organizations working on transparency and monitoring of the health sector and its actors. BHW plays an important area for strengthening the voice of women and the public as well as demanding responsibility from the government and other decision makers. This is Sida's second project with BHW. The project will continue to promote a responsive health system with greater focus on accountability, including anti-corruption, especially at the local level. The proposed project will have three strategic objectives: 1) Strengthened local level accountability. 2) Strengthened media engagement and capacity to promote social accountability in health. 3) Strengthened advocacy work to accelerate the implementation of universal health coverage (UHC) by the government. During the proposed phase, local health forums of volunteers, will be a key vehicle to achieve stronger social accountability. Linked to this work, policy advocacy at the central level by the secretariat will complement.

Bangladesh Health Watch (BHW) är en civilsamhällesorganisation som arbetar med transparens och ansvarsutkrävande inom hälsosektorn. BHW spelar en viktig roll i att stärka medborgares röst gentemot regeringen och andra beslutsfattare, med ett särskilt fokus på kvinnligt deltagande. Detta är Sidas andra projekt med BHW. Projektet kommer att fortsätta att främja ett responsivt hälsosystem med större fokus på ansvarsutkrävande, inklusive anti-korruption, särskilt på lokal nivå. Projektet kommer att arbeta mot tre strategiska mål: 1) Stärkt ansvar på lokal nivå. 2) Stärkt medieengagemang och kapacitet att främja socialt ansvarstagande inom hälsa. 3) Stärkt påverkansarbete för att påskynda implementeringen av universell hälsotäckning (UHC) av regeringen. Under den föreslagna fasen kommer lokala hälsoforum, som samlar volontärer, att vara en en viktig plattform för att stärka socialt ansvarsutkrävande. Kopplat till detta arbete, kommer påverkansarbete koordineras av sekretariatet på nationell nivå.

The vision is that all citizens of Bangladesh enjoy universal health care (UHC) and the mission is to build a functional platform through which citizens and all other relevant stakeholders of the country can get their voices heard and thereby influence policies and programmes impacting citizen's health.
The overall goal is to contribute to increasing the health and productivity of the citizens of Bangladesh.
The proposed project will have three strategic objectives:
Objective 1: Strengthened local-level accountability
1.1 Systematise and strengthen public hearing and authority meetings
1.2 Institutionalise facility monitoring by Regional Chapter (RC) members
1.3 Strengthen RCs including Youth Forums
1.4 Enhance Host Organisation (HO) capacity and interest to support Regional Chapters
1.5 Strengthen ownership of RCs and HOs for sustainability
1.6 Improve attendance of service providers in health centres
Expected outcomes:
- Stronger RC platform to claim local level accountability from health service delivery system
- Concrete plan for post-project sustainability of initiatives at local level developed
- Improved quality of services at local level
- Increased people's voice
Objective 2: Strengthened media engagement and capacity to promote social accountability in health
2.1 Expand and strengthen local-level media partnership
2.2 Strengthen national-level media partnership
Expected outcomes:
- Increased participation of local journalists in social accountability activities (public hearings, campaigns, rallies)
- Increased coverage and impact of media reporting on health issues
Objective 3: Strengthened advocacy work to accelerate the implementation of UHC by the government
3.1 Evidence based advocacy for increased allocation to PHC in health budget
3.2 Use legal provisions for improving quality of specific areas of health services (Public Interest Litigation)
3.3 Facilitate the work of Anti-Corruption platform working on absenteeism and reducing medicine prices
Expected outcomes:
- Increased allocation for PHC in health sector budget
- High Court directives on selected issues of public health importance operationalized
- Public opinion created and policymakers mobilised to reduce absenteeism in government facilities and reduce medicine prices
The target group
The direct beneficiaries of the project will be the citizens of Bangladesh, especially the catchment's population (approx 15 million) of the eight Regional Chapters. The indirect beneficiaries will the health managers, service providers, and members of the various tiers for Regional Chapters.

sector.narrative: Media and free flow of information

description.narrative:
Objective 1: Strengthened Local-Level Accountability
There are indications that the project advanced local-level health accountability across its Regional Chapters (RCs), with improvements in service responsiveness, transparency, and civic engagement.
- Improved responsiveness of health authorities: Through 10 district-level multi-stakeholder public hearings and 16 formal meetings between Forums and hospital authorities, community members were able to raise service-related concerns directly with high-level health officials. These dialogues led to real-time commitments to address issues such as absenteeism, facility readiness, and service gaps.
- Systematic monitoring and follow-up: RC members conducted annual facility performance reviews, identifying specific quality gaps and following up with responsible authorities. The process has institutionalized a cycle of community-based monitoring and corrective action in health service delivery.
- Strengthened community-level platforms: A total of 37 coordination meetings were held at Community Clinics and Union Health and Family Welfare Centres (UHFWCs), effectively activating previously dormant management committees. These meetings resulted in localized problem-solving and community ownership of facility-level issues.
- Youth engagement and leadership: Youth Forums increased their visibility and effectiveness by participating in monitoring visits, conducting awareness campaigns, and supporting vulnerable populations. Their proactive roles in disaster response (e.g., flood relief, free medical camps) and blood donation drives strengthened their credibility and embedded them as long-term stakeholders in local accountability mechanisms.
- Emergence of autonomous civic actions: RCs in districts such as Khagrachhari, Netrakona, and Manikganj demonstrated initiative beyond project mandatesadvocating for clinic relocations, equipping facilities, and supporting marginalized groups. This evolution from activity-based engagement to autonomous advocacy is a strong indicator of sustainable local accountability.
Examples from Sunamganj
In Sunamganj, the district Health Rights Forum (HRF) introduced a citizens charter that provides clear information about the services available at the local clinic, such as malaria and dengue testing. This intervention has had a noticeable impact: the number of patients visiting the Sripur clinic has doubled, increasing from around 250 to approximately 500 patients per month. Alongside this growth, the quality of services at the clinic has also improved. Regular meetings between the community group committee and clinic staff have encouraged the doctor to increase his presence at the facility, further strengthening care provision.
Building on previous efforts, the district HRF has driven several significant improvements in the area. These include electrifying the Sripur Clinic and restoring a dilapidated road connecting it to the Lakhmansri Family Welfare Centre. Similar achievements have been recorded in other regions, such as securing water connections, installing tube wells, and providing medical equipment to health care facilities.
The HRF has also actively collaborated with local residents to resist corrupt practices that hinder access to health care. These include challenges posed by private ambulance syndicates and widespread doctor absenteeism. Through ongoing dialogue with both doctors and ambulance providers, patients have reported fewer cases of doctors prioritizing their private practices over public duties, and exploitative behaviors by private ambulances are increasingly being challenged.
Objective 2: Strengthened Media Engagement and Capacity to Promote Social Accountability in Health
The project has enhanced both the capacity and reach of media actors in health accountability discourse.
Increased quantity and quality of health journalism: Following targeted training workshops held in October and November 2024, local journalists from multiple RCs produced and published investigative reports highlighting systemic issues such as absenteeism, drug pricing, and local service failures. The publication of these reports in mainstream and regional outlets has broadened public understanding and pressure for reform.
Stronger media-health sector interface: A national-level workshop on investigative health journalism, held in July 2024, equipped 27 journalists with thematic expertise and advanced reporting skills. This capacity-building resulted in direct media outputs on topics like antimicrobial resistance and informal payment practicesissues previously under-reported.
Strategic alliances with national media actors: BHWs collaboration with national-level outlets led to increased visibility of underrepresented health issues. This partnership has established a media feedback loop that aligns journalistic outputs with citizen grievances and policy advocacy.
Institutionalized journalist engagement: The creation and activation of Health Reporters Forums and consistent involvement of journalists in public hearings and policy dialogues have institutionalized media as an integral actor in health accountability efforts.
Objective 3: Strengthened Advocacy Work to Accelerate the Implementation of UHC by the Government
The project achieved significant milestones in evidence-based and legal advocacy, influencing both policy discussions and institutional reforms.
Local health budget tracking for policy influence: A study analyzing local-level health budget allocations in Kurigram district has been completed and is now being disseminated. Findings from the study are expected to serve as a foundation for evidence-driven advocacy on increasing health care spending, notably on primary health care.
Structured dialogues on absenteeism and retention: Through eight district-level workshops with health managers and service providers, actionable recommendations were developed to address absenteeism and workforce retention. These regional dialogues have created a channel for ground-level insights to inform national policy processes. BHW are now preparing for a national policy dialogue to present regional findings. A draft action plan on absenteeism will be shared with the development partner anti-corruption coalition, headed by Sweden, ensuring coordinated advocacy efforts.
National policy momentum through legal mechanisms: The projects engagement in Public Interest Litigations (PILs) has resulted in tangible institutional commitments, particularly in road traffic emergency care and C-section regulationissues central to Universal Health Coverage (UHC) equity and access goals. However, these commitments are yet to be translated into action.
- Caesarean Section (C-section) guidelines endorsed by the High Court were translated into Bangla, facilitating public access and understanding. The process signifies the successful completion of a legal advocacy cyclefrom petition to policy change to public dissemination.
- Emergency Services Protocol for Road Crash Victims was developed, endorsed by the Ministry of Health, and is now pending piloting. This protocol addresses a major service gap in pre-hospital trauma care and marks a concrete policy outcome with the potential to transform emergency medical response in Bangladesh.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
